name: Arc
executive_summary: Arc launched its public mainnet on September 16, 2026, built by Circle as an institutional layer-1 running on Malachite, a Byzantine fault-tolerant consensus engine originally built for Tendermint and CometBFT. It's an EVM-compatible chain that runs entirely on USDC as its gas token, secured by permissioned validator institutions including BlackRock, DTCC, Visa, and Mastercard. First scored September 17, 2026 at one to two days old, the chain was reassessed at one month on October 18, 2026. Two categories moved: Real-World Utility rose from 32 to 36 and KYA from 28 to 34, lifting the TradFi score from 38 to 39 and the AI score from 44 to 45, with both tiers unchanged. TradFi Approved holds at 74 on the validator roster, while On-Chain Health stays at 13 and Tokenomics & Supply at 20, since the ARC token is still minted but not tradeable, staked, or governing anything, and on-chain research shows much of the early activity is concentrated in a few wallets. The result is an extraordinary institutional foundation with a still-thin, partly non-organic usage record, and no independent audit of the core protocol yet.

key_findings: TradFi Approved scores 74, one of Arc's clearest strengths: the validators securing this chain are institutions like BlackRock, DTCC, Visa, Mastercard, ICE, and Standard Chartered, not partners or sponsors but the literal infrastructure of the network, confirmed by an independent on-chain read rather than a press release. The score sits below what that roster alone might suggest because the chain's operating record is one month long, and this framework weights a track record built over years more heavily than one built over weeks.

On-Chain Health scores 13, unchanged at one month. Headline USDC balances and lending deposits have grown, but independent on-chain research finds them highly concentrated: 24 addresses hold about 92% of the chain's roughly $600 million in USDC, six borrowers account for about 73% of the largest lending market's debt (much of it borrowed and immediately bridged off the chain), at least 32% of post-launch wallets trace to a small number of funding clusters, and a single wallet trading against its own liquidity produced about 38% of one month's DEX volume. User activity also fell sharply after the launch spike. That is not yet the kind of organic track record this category rewards.

Real-World Utility scores 36, up from 32. Two Janus Henderson funds (JAAA and JTRSY) and a New York Life high-yield bond product (HYB) went live on Arc through Centrifuge on October 2, 2026, joining the one institutional fund already deployed at the first scoring. These are deployed and subscribable, but each is restricted to eligible non-U.S. institutional investors with high minimums, and no Arc-specific subscription volume or holder data has been published for the new products. BlackRock's BUIDL is still not confirmed as deployed on this chain. The credit for the new products is partly offset by the concentration findings above, which show the DeFi-liquidity leg of this category to be more concentrated and transient than it first appeared.

Tokenomics & Supply scores 20. Ten billion ARC tokens were minted at genesis with a disclosed 60/25/15 allocation, but the token is not tradeable, not staked, not used for gas, and does not govern anything. Circle's own materials describe the genesis mint as "not a commitment to publicly launch." The chain's actual transactional currency is USDC, Circle's own stablecoin, which carries no economic exposure to whether this network succeeds or fails.

Decentralization scores 47. The validator set read at 15 active validators at first scoring, with the largest holding 7.69% of voting power, a reasonably even split for a set this size, but only 5 of the 15 are needed to halt the network and only 9 to break its safety threshold. No change to the validator cohort has been reported since launch.

Security & Future-Proofing scores 22. Arc runs an active bug bounty that found and fixed a real consensus-layer vulnerability before mainnet launched, and recent payouts have been small, with no post-launch critical protocol disclosure found. But no independent audit of the chain's core protocol or its Malachite consensus layer has been published, and the protocol's own repository describes its software as alpha and not externally audited. A month of operation without a reported halt, reorg, or consensus incident is useful context, but it is a short record rather than a track record.

Regulatory & Risk scores 68. No enforcement action and no adverse classification exist against this chain or its token, compliance tooling from established providers is built in, and the operating company itself holds a federal trust charter and is separately publicly listed. The only distribution of the ARC token to date was a closed institutional presale to accredited investors, a minor note at this category's weight rather than a material risk.

Execution Layer scores 62. Transactions finalize in under a second with no reported congestion, and deterministic finality means the chain has no fork-choice reorgs by design. Fees are priced in USD-pegged USDC rather than a volatile native token, which matters for automated systems that need predictable costs. The open question is real load: day-one throughput was roughly 90 transactions per second against a stated design target above 3,000, so performance well beyond that remains untested.

Composability & Atomicity scores 68. Standard batching and permit tools (Multicall3, Permit2, a CREATE2 factory) are confirmed live at their expected addresses, and the chain shipped its own precompiles that let a batched call preserve the original caller's identity, solving an attribution problem most general-purpose EVM chains leave unsolved. The one gap: a smart-account factory address is still not listed in the chain's own official documentation, even though custody providers claim support.

Security Posture scores 15. No independent audit of the core protocol exists, and an outside technical review flagged that both the execution client and the consensus client run as a single implementation each, a double point of failure. Layered on top is validator concentration (15 validators at first scoring, the largest holding 7.69%) and an operating record of one month. An active bug bounty that already caught one real vulnerability before launch, and a month with no reported halt or consensus incident, are the things working in this category's favor.

Economic Predictability scores 35. Gas priced in USD-pegged USDC is a genuine plus for an automated system that can't tolerate volatile costs. Working against it: block production is entirely permissioned, and the chain has a live, enforced protocol-level mechanism that can block specific addresses from moving USDC, with no published commitment from any validator not to use it. No documented production use of that mechanism against an external address has been found.

Agent Tooling scores 45. Real, chain-specific infrastructure for autonomous agents exists rather than borrowed generic EVM tooling: agent wallets with policy limits, a small-payments mechanism, an agent marketplace, and a payment-facilitator service. Small early agent usage is observable, such as tiny USDC bounty payouts, but no verified material agent-driven volume exists, the agent platforms said to be building here are announced rather than confirmed as live traffic, and a fair-ordering overlay for agents remains at the research and design-partner stage.

Standards & Interoperability scores 58. Account abstraction is more than a compatibility claim here: the chain operator's own production wallet is built as a smart-contract account with real operational monitoring, and a native token-bridging mechanism avoids the custody risk of a typical lock-and-mint bridge. Held back because the canonical account-abstraction entry-point address is still not published anywhere official.

KYA scores 34, up from 28. All three ERC-8004 agent registries (Identity, Reputation, and Validation) are now deployed on mainnet, confirmed against the chain's official contract-address reference and the block explorer, where the Validation registry shows verified proxy code. Early registration is real but thin, roughly 185 agent identities as of late September 2026, concentrated across a few dozen owners, and the Validation registry has seen only a handful of transactions. No major AI agent platform is using the stack at production scale. This is a live identity pathway with early adoption, not broad adoption.

watch_items: The ARC token itself is the single biggest swing factor. No staking, no live governance, no confirmed fee-burn mechanics, and no public launch date exist today. Any of those becoming live would be a direct re-credit candidate for Tokenomics & Supply.

Three institutional real-world-asset products (JAAA, JTRSY, HYB) are now live but gated to eligible non-U.S. institutions, and BlackRock's BUIDL is not confirmed as deployed. Published subscription volume or holder data, or BUIDL actually deploying, would be a re-credit candidate for Real-World Utility.

No independent audit of the core protocol exists. A published, scoped audit would be a direct re-credit candidate on both the security-posture gate and both axes' security categories. The chain's December 2025 materials reference ongoing audits of parts of the stack, but no firm, scope, or report is public.

Independent research finds USDC balances, lending debt, and DEX volume concentrated in a small number of wallets and funding clusters. Broader, more organic distribution of activity would be a re-credit candidate for On-Chain Health.

A live, enforced protocol-level mechanism can block specific addresses from moving USDC. Any documented production use against an external address would be a further consideration at the next reassessment.

The ERC-8004 Validation registry is deployed but has seen almost no use, and the smart-account factory and entry-point addresses are still unpublished. Adoption by a production agent platform, or those addresses being published, would be a re-credit candidate for KYA and Standards & Interoperability.

This chain was reassessed at one month on October 18, 2026. The next reassessment should check the ARC token's status, audit progress, validator concentration, and whether usage broadens beyond the current concentrated wallets.

tiles.cheapest_tx_cost_note: Not yet determined. Gas is paid in USDC, but pricing data for this chain is not yet tracked by the fee-data sources this board uses. A read is planned at the next reassessment.
tiles.fee_yield_note: Not measurable. This metric divides fee revenue by market cap, and the ARC token has no live market or market cap to divide by -- the chain's actual gas token, USDC, is not an investable asset this metric is designed to measure.
